name: Dorik
tagline: Build a small responsive site with pages, collections, and simple forms

tiers.name: Personal
tiers.limits: 1 custom domain; 25 static pages; 200 blog posts; 5 CMS collections and 200 collection items; no collaborators
tiers.notes: $249/year. A two-year commitment is advertised at $10.38/month equivalent; a separate $249 one-time lifetime offer was also live.

tiers.name: Business
tiers.limits: 3 custom domains; unlimited pages/blog posts/storage/bandwidth; 10 collaborators
tiers.notes: $498/year. A two-year commitment is advertised at $20.75/month equivalent; a separate $599 one-time lifetime offer was also live.

tiers.name: Agency
tiers.limits: Unlimited custom domains, pages, collaborators, blog posts, storage and bandwidth; agency white-label/client-billing features
tiers.notes: $948/year; two-year and lifetime pricing are contact-sales/custom.

pricing.freeTierCaps: no free tier; 7-day trial, with site count determined by the trialed plan
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual; separate two-year and limited-time lifetime purchase options are also advertised
pricing.hiddenCosts: Dorik does not sell domains; you must buy one separately. Lifetime Personal charges $199 one-time per additional website; Lifetime Business charges $149 per additional website and limits code export to 15/month.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For Dorik, build a small responsive site with pages, collections, and simple forms. The hard boundary is hosting, cms, memberships, templates, and no-code editing polish, plus editor polish, hosting, templates, and ecosystem.
coreLoopDIY: Assemble a small responsive site from sections with pages, collections, and simple forms, edit copy and media, preview breakpoints, and publish a static site to a user-owned target.
whatYouLose: hosting, CMS, memberships, templates, and no-code editing polish
moatNotes: editor polish, hosting, templates, and ecosystem
ongoingBurden: responsive rendering, forms, domains, certificates, deploys, backups, template maintenance, and browser regressions
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Dorik because the page renderer is reproducible, but customers pay to avoid becoming their own hosting and browser-compatibility team. The recurring cost buys responsive rendering, forms, domains, certificates, deploys, backups, template maintenance, and browser regressions, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Webstudio
priorArt.desc: Open-source visual website builder designed around web standards.

alternatives.name: Concrete CMS
alternatives.desc: A proper in-page CMS for people who prefer editing the page to editing a dashboard about the page.

facts.install: Release ZIP to PHP hosting, create a MySQL/MariaDB database, then finish the browser installer
facts.dataFormat: Pages, users, settings and block data in SQL; uploaded assets in the server file manager or a configured remote storage location
facts.gapVsPaid: Concrete CMS is less visually freeform and polished than Dorik, and the owner must provide hosting, updates, backups and form delivery.
facts.setupBlocker: PHP hosting, a database, writable directories, and responsibility for updates, backups and outbound mail

alternatives.name: Microweber
alternatives.desc: A drag-and-drop PHP CMS with pages, forms and collections; simple to edit, not maintenance-free.

facts.install: Hosted signup, or upload the PHP package to a web host and complete its browser installer
facts.dataFormat: Site content and settings in a supported SQL database; images and other uploads in server storage
facts.gapVsPaid: Microweber's templates and integrations are less polished, and replacing Dorik means running the PHP host, updates, backups and mail yourself.
facts.setupBlocker: Self-hosting needs compatible PHP extensions, URL rewriting, a database and correct filesystem permissions

alternatives.name: Plasmic
alternatives.desc: Unlimited hosted projects, CMS and custom domains free; the badge is cheaper than Dorik.

facts.install: Hosted signup; optional npm-installed Plasmic CLI for React code generation and deployment in your own repository
facts.engines: Plasmic AI (beta); the official site does not name its underlying model provider
facts.dataFormat: Hosted projects and CMS records in Plasmic Cloud; codegen writes React components plus plasmic.json and plasmic.lock into the user's repository
facts.gapVsPaid: Plasmic is much more React/component-oriented than Dorik, and its free hosted output keeps Plasmic branding.
facts.setupBlocker: Free hosted output keeps Plasmic branding; codegen/self-deployment requires a Node/React project and deployment workflow

alternatives.name: Silex
alternatives.desc: A visual multi-page static-site builder with export; collections are manual rather than magical.

facts.install: Use the hosted editor with a GitLab login, install the desktop alpha, or run the official Docker setup
facts.engines: Optional desktop MCP workflow can connect to Ollama, OpenCode, Goose or Claude Code
facts.dataFormat: Project JSON and assets in GitLab, FTP or local storage; publishing produces ordinary static HTML, CSS and JavaScript
facts.gapVsPaid: Silex has no comparable built-in collections/CMS workflow, so repeated content and simple data-driven pages become manual.
facts.setupBlocker: The stable hosted route starts with a GitLab account; the desktop build is still labelled alpha

alternatives.name: Vvveb
alternatives.desc: A finished visual CMS with forms, posts and custom content; obscure enough that support starts with reading docs.

facts.install: Download and upload the PHP release, open the site URL, and complete the browser installer
facts.dataFormat: Content, products, orders and settings in MySQL/MariaDB, SQLite or PostgreSQL; media and downloadable files on the server filesystem
facts.gapVsPaid: Vvveb is less polished and approachable than Dorik, and the reader becomes responsible for the PHP server, mail, security and backups.
facts.setupBlocker: PHP hosting, a database, writable files, mail and payment configuration, plus ongoing server updates

alternatives.name: Webstudio
alternatives.desc: A polished visual builder and CMS connector; using your own domain for free moves hosting onto you.

facts.install: Hosted signup or desktop app; alternatively export the project or deploy the self-hosted builder/site
facts.engines: Webstudio Inception AI and MCP integrations; the hosted model provider is not named in official documentation
facts.dataFormat: Projects and assets live in Webstudio Cloud when hosted there; export/self-host routes produce source or static assets under the user's deployment
facts.gapVsPaid: Webstudio lacks Dorik's all-in-one collections/forms/hosting simplicity, and a free custom-domain site requires export or self-hosting.
facts.setupBlocker: The free cloud plan publishes only to a Webstudio subdomain; a free custom domain requires export or self-hosting

rejectedAlternatives.name: GrapesJS
rejectedAlternatives.desc: The editor is real; the product around it is yours to build.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Personal plan and a single-site builder DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Dorik in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, SQLite, Drizzle ORM, and static export; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: assemble a small responsive site from sections with pages, collections, and simple forms, edit copy and media, preview breakpoints, and publish a static site to a user-owned target.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Provide a section library for hero, proof, features, pricing, FAQ, and footer blocks.
Use a constrained design-token system rather than arbitrary CSS controls.
Allow inline text editing and local image upload with responsive optimization.
Preview desktop, tablet, and mobile widths and surface overflow errors.
Persist projects in SQLite and support a portable JSON export.
Generate a clean static Next.js output and document deployment to one target.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out a plugin marketplace.
Deliberately leave out multi-tenant managed hosting.
Deliberately leave out advanced ecommerce, memberships, and agency billing.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
